props.title: Conquest

sections.content: Conquest stands as one of Greta Garbo's most ambitious historical dramas, depicting Napoleon's tumultuous relationship with Polish countess Marie Walewska. The film showcases MGM's lavish production values of the 1930s, with stunning costume design by Adrian and atmospheric cinematography by Karl Freund. Like other prestigious MGM historical epics like Queen Christina (1933) and Marie Antoinette (1938), Conquest blends romantic melodrama with political intrigue, though its somber tone and focus on Napoleon's decline sets it apart from more triumphant biopics of the era.

sections.content: The film's portrayal of Napoleon by Charles Boyer represents a fascinating departure from typical Hollywood depictions of the French emperor. Unlike the more bombastic characterization in Désirée (1954) with Marlon Brando, Boyer plays Napoleon with subtle complexity - showing both the calculated political strategist and the vulnerable lover. Director Clarence Brown, who frequently collaborated with Garbo, creates intimate scenes between the leads that feel surprisingly modern in their psychological complexity.

The film's production history reveals MGM's determination to maintain its reputation for prestigious historical dramas. Following the success of Romeo and Juliet (1936), the studio spared no expense, spending over $2.7 million - an enormous sum for 1937. The attention to historical detail, from the recreation of Napoleonic-era Warsaw to the intricate military uniforms, set a standard for accuracy that would influence later historical epics like War and Peace (1956). sections.content: Conquest fits into a long tradition of Napoleonic cinema that includes Abel Gance's groundbreaking Napoleon (1927) and Sacha Guitry's Napoleon (1955). The film's focus on Napoleon's personal life rather than his military campaigns anticipated later works like The Young Napoleon (1969) and Ridley Scott's Napoleon (2023). Each iteration reflects its era's understanding of the historical figure, with Conquest's emphasis on romantic tragedy speaking to 1930s audiences' appetite for historical melodrama.
